summary: Reports on a 2019 workshop convened by the Internet Architecture Board on the gap between how protocols are designed to behave and how they behave once deployed. It summarizes the main discussion points and suggests topics for further consideration. The views are those of participants, not an IETF consensus.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts talked about how Internet designs often work out differently in the real world than planned, and this is the meeting write-up.

questions: why do protocols behave differently in deployment
subtitle: How Internet protocols often deploy in unexpected, centralized ways

tldr.problem: Internet protocols are designed with assumptions about how they will be deployed—like email being decentralized, DNS being hierarchical, and the Web being distributed. In practice, deployments often become highly centralized due to economics, security, or market forces.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board convened a 2019 workshop to investigate cases where deployment reality diverged from design expectations. Participants submitted 21 position papers and discussed patterns in concentration, security implications, and what designers should do differently.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified that centralization is often driven by business models, DDoS resilience, and regulatory preferences. It recommended that the IETF focus on open interfaces, data minimization, and interoperability standards to counter unwanted concentration.

today: RFC 8980 is an Informational report from the Internet Architecture Board documenting a June 2019 workshop. It presents the workshop participants' consensus views, not IETF or IAB positions, but captures expert opinion on a critical architectural issue: the tendency for Internet protocols designed for distribution to become concentrated in practice. The report remains current as these architectural tensions persist.

sections.title: Design Expectations vs. Deployment Reality
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) holds periodic workshops on long-term Internet issues. This 2019 workshop examined a specific problem: protocols are designed with assumptions about deployment models that often fail to materialize in practice.

For example, email was presumed to run on many independent providers in an uncoordinated fashion. In reality, consolidation combined with the need for coordinated spam defense has created massive concentration. DNS was designed for deep hierarchies but is often deployed in large, flat zones where nameservers become critical infrastructure. Future DNS may see further concentration through globally available resolver services, creating both benefits (better security and performance) and risks (privacy concerns and single points of failure).

The Web is fundamentally decentralized but now relies on Content Delivery Networks for distribution and DDoS defense. Smaller operators find it impractical to compete without using a global commercial service. Machine learning is creating similar issues: distributing effective ML deployment is difficult, favoring centralized providers.

The workshop brought together 30 participants to identify patterns in how and why these divergences occur, and to explore what the IETF and Internet architecture community can do about them.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers built the Internet to be open and spread out, but it keeps getting pulled toward a few big companies that run critical services.

sections.title: Past Experiences and Lessons
sections.content:
The workshop examined many cases: WebPKI (certificate authorities) became heavily concentrated; DNSSEC struggled to deploy while easier alternatives succeeded; BGP remains problematic despite known security issues; Network Address Translators (NATs) became ubiquitous despite being considered temporary; DNS resolvers centralized; Content Delivery Networks became essential infrastructure; and Internet of Things manufacturers set low security expectations.

Several patterns emerged. Feedback from deployers comes too late in the design process. Building blocks get repurposed in unexpected ways, and user communities join discussions too late. The Web has become increasingly centralized, and it is unclear what technical path leads to better distribution.

Strong forces push toward centralization: deployment is easier in a centralized model, business and regulatory processes prefer a small set of well-defined entities to negotiate with, and regulators often prefer to talk to a small number of major providers rather than a diverse ecosystem.

The workshop noted that it is difficult to predict how useful new protocols will be and challenging for the IETF to interact with other communities (business sectors like aviation and healthcare, or regulators) that need new technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Real networks do not behave like the plan. Companies find it easier to centralize. Regulators like talking to three companies instead of thirty. And everyone involved with the design learns too late what people actually want.

sections.title: Underlying Principles and Forces
sections.content:
The workshop identified several principles that explain deployment divergence. First-mover advantage is powerful: when one technology is already deployed and provides most benefits, alternatives struggle even if technically superior. WebPKI succeeded where DNSSEC did not, partly due to earlier commercial adoption.

Deployment failures tend to happen when interdependencies make progress difficult and there is no immediate advantage for early adoption. BGP has known security gaps, but deploying improvements requires coordinated change across many networks with no obvious short-term benefit.

Another pattern is that success is difficult to predict. In fact, preventing wild success may be the only way to control deployments—but wild success is what we want. This creates a paradox.

The workshop discussed different deployment patterns. Some services are delivered as web applications where the infrastructure is open but the service is closed (two components of the same provider's software competing over the Internet). Others deliver concentrated network services (mail, DNS resolution) that offer standard Internet capabilities.

Centralization often comes from business models that make concentrated provision easier (economies of scale), DDoS resilience only a few large providers can achieve, regulatory preferences for dealing with a small number of known entities, and commercial surveillance opportunities created by centralization.
sections.plainLanguage: The first popular choice often wins even if later choices are better. When nobody benefits from switching, nothing changes. Success is hard to predict, so you cannot plan to prevent concentration.

sections.title: The Centralization Problem
sections.content:
Centralization creates significant risks to user choice, privacy, and future protocol evolution. The workshop spent considerable time on this core issue. When a service (like DNS queries or email) becomes concentrated in a few providers, those providers have power over what users see and can do, and they can change the service in ways that harm privacy or stifle competition.

DDoS defense was identified as a particularly important driver of centralization. DNS systems can face overwhelming attack traffic that only the largest providers can absorb. This pushes users toward concentrated, commercial resolver services.

The workshop identified some potential counterbalances. Layered defenses and federation can provide DDoS resilience without centralization. Data object encryption and refusing to store all data in one place can protect privacy. Open interfaces are crucial: as long as specific functions have well-defined, open APIs, other parties can perform them, preventing bundling into one large provider.

Browsers are increasingly important: competition in the browser market can push for privacy-protecting changes. However, this requires browser vendors to act on behalf of users, and current commercial surveillance is not well curbed by existing means.
sections.plainLanguage: When three companies run all the DNS in the world, they can see what everyone is looking up. If you make the interfaces between services public and open, anyone can build an alternative service.

sections.title: Security Implications and Future Actions
sections.content:
The workshop concluded that a modern threat model is needed. In the past, security concerns were mostly about communications—were packets encrypted and authenticated? Modern systems face different threats: endpoints may be malicious, centralized infrastructure is an attractive target for surveillance, and trusting endpoints is harder.

The participants agreed that non-communications-security issues need to be addressed: data minimization, endpoint authentication, and infrastructure diversity.

For future action, the workshop identified three main architectural outputs: (1) develop and document a modern threat model that includes endpoints and centralization; (2) continue discussion of consolidation and centralization issues; (3) document architectural principles, such as re-application of the end-to-end principle.

Specific IETF work should include taking reputation systems into account, ensuring certificate scoping can be limited, building end-to-end encryption tools for applications, and documenting deployment assumptions in working group charters.

The workshop emphasized that the IETF should focus on what it controls (standards and protocols) while being available as an expert to other discussions. The best way to make an impact is through standards work, not abstract discussions. Concrete, practical actions—determining how to make a specific service better—are more useful than abstract principles.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet design needs to consider not just eavesdropping but also malicious endpoints and concentrated companies. The IETF should write standards that make open interfaces and competition possible.
